name: Karl Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Karl, 27, and I live with my partner Lena in a flat over a bakery on Station Road. She's training as a hairdresser, so money's tight on both sides right now. I work at Halvorsen, the appliance factory, in the sheet metal shop. Started there five months ago, after a couple of years in a tyre-fitting place.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a press brake, which is a big machine that bends flat steel sheets into the sides and tops of washing machines. I load the sheets, line them up against the back gauge, press the pedal, check the angle and stack them. I'm still slow at the setups, and Ingrid, the cell leader, has caught me bending a whole stack the wrong way round once already. I like it though, I'm a hands person, and on my phone at break I ask an AI to explain the bending tables, which has helped me catch up faster than the training sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, honestly, because I get a lot out of it. I'd probably still tell the guys at break to try it for the small stuff. Online I'd say people overhyped it, but it's still the best tool I've got on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job carries on as it is, which is fine, it's a real job. I'd keep using AI for learning and for my side thing, I fix up second-hand e-bikes and sell them online. It writes my listings and helps me find faults, so even a modest AI is useful to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it with Ingrid and try to be signed off on setups by spring. I'd grow the e-bike thing a bit, maybe do two a month instead of one, which is an extra hundred and fifty or so. That money would go into savings, because right now we've got about two weeks of bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, because I like things changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a recent e-bike.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I got one with a dead battery for sixty from a guy clearing out his garage. I asked the AI what the error code on the display meant, turned out it was a loose connector, not the battery. Cleaned it, new brake pads, sold it for two hundred and thirty. That paid our electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there robots at Halvorsen already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's one robot press brake cell on the far side of the shop, with an arm that loads it. It does the long runs of the same part. Ingrid says it's fussy and needs a person nearby to sort it out, which is the job I'd want eventually.

S0.say: He'd say it's a shame AI plateaued because he gets a lot from it, and he'd still tell co-workers to try it. Online he'd say it was overhyped but remains the best tool on his phone.
S0.think: He thinks his factory job carries on, which is fine. AI still helps him learn and run his side business fixing and selling used e-bikes.
S0.do: Works towards being signed off on setups by spring and doubles his e-bike sales to two a month, adding about a hundred and fifty. Puts that extra into savings, which currently cover about two weeks of bills.
S0.feel: Calm, maybe a little flat because he likes change.
S0.quote: Turned out it was a loose connector, not the battery. Cleaned it, new brake pads, sold it for two hundred and thirty. That paid our electricity.
S0.fieldNote: Karl already uses AI daily in practical ways, both at work and in a small e-bike side business. A plateau barely affects him and even disappoints him a little. He's already eyeing the robot cell as his next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way things are going, so the sensible thing is to get ahead of it. At work I'd tell people, learn the robot cell, don't wait to be told. I'm not going to blame anyone, companies are going to do what makes sense for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's an opening for me. If more of the shop goes robotic, they'll need people who can set up and babysit the robot cells, and I'm young and I pick things up. The risk is I'm only five months in, so I've got to move before they hire someone trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd ask Ingrid if I can spend my overtime on the robot cell, learning the teach pendant, which is the handheld controller you program it with. I'd use the AI to go through the manufacturer's manuals in the evenings. Then I'd apply for the first robot cell operator post that opened, and if Halvorsen didn't have one, I'd look at the car parts plant over in Ashby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. A bit of a buzz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move plants with two weeks of savings. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. But staying put in a job that's shrinking is risky too, it's just slower. I'd line up the new job before leaving, and I'd keep the e-bikes going as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in the e-bike business as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Already do, but I'd go further. I'd get it to track which models sell fastest and set my prices, and maybe set up an online shop so I'm not just on the marketplace sites. It saves me hours I'd otherwise spend typing.

S1.say: He'd say the sensible move is to get ahead of the change and tell co-workers to learn the robot cell without waiting. He wouldn't blame companies for doing what makes sense for them.
S1.think: Privately he sees it as an opening, since robot cells need people to set them up and watch them, and he learns fast. His worry is being too new and losing out to a trained outside hire.
S1.do: Spends his overtime learning the robot cell's handheld controller and studies the manuals with AI at night. Applies for the first robot cell operator post, at Halvorsen or a car parts plant nearby, and uses AI to price and track sales in his e-bike business.
S1.feel: Good, with a bit of a buzz.
S1.quote: Staying put in a job that's shrinking is risky too, it's just slower.
S1.fieldNote: Karl treats moderate change as a door opening and plans within the first week. He doesn't blame employers at all. Even with very thin savings he's willing to switch plants, cushioned by his side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, nobody's ready, so let's not pretend. The government needs to keep people afloat while it sorts itself out. I'd probably say it in a calmer way than most people, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my factory job goes and so does the robot cell job, because the robots would set themselves up. The e-bike thing might last a bit longer, people still like buying from a person. But two years with two weeks of savings is scary, I won't pretend it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every bit of extra out of the next two years: overtime, more e-bikes, sell the van and get a cheaper one. In the first months after it lands I'd try to be the person who sets up the new robots for small workshops, the ones that can't afford engineers, while that window exists. I'd use the AI for everything, quotes, adverts, learning, because it'd be stupid not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, a lot more than the others. But I'd feel like I was moving, not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long do you think that window would last, setting up robots for small workshops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I don't know. Maybe a year, maybe two. It's a guess. But you take the gap while it's there and you save every penny, because it's the last gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight that I'd be working stupid hours for a while. She'd probably say, what about your back, because I'm already sore from the press brake. And I'd say, we can rest when there's something to rest on.

S2.say: He'd say nobody is ready and the government needs to keep people afloat while things settle. He'd say it more calmly than most.
S2.think: He believes both his factory job and the robot cell role would go, while his e-bike business might last a little longer. Two years with two weeks of savings scares him.
S2.do: Squeezes the next two years for overtime and e-bike sales and swaps his van for a cheaper one. After AGI lands, offers robot set-up to small workshops while that window lasts, using AI for quotes, adverts and learning.
S2.feel: Much more nervous than in the slower pictures, but moving rather than stuck.
S2.quote: You take the gap while it's there and you save every penny, because it's the last gap.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture he looks for a short-lived opening rather than shutting down. He's honest that the window is a guess. His centrist view still bends to wanting government support when everyone is hit at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, so make one. I'd tell people at work to learn the robots now, while they still need us to run them. I'd say it without any drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32. I think I'd get three or four good years out of robot cells and set-ups, maybe more if I start my own small business doing it. After that, I don't know, but I'd have money behind me for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the robot cell at Halvorsen in year one and do a short course in robot programming, the kind you can do at weekends. By year two I'd set up a small side business installing and fixing small robot arms for local workshops. I'd save hard, at least two hundred a month once it's going, and keep the e-bikes for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, but mostly busy and kind of excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably we'd wait on having kids. We'd talked about maybe at 30. With this coming, I'd want two or three years of good money saved first, so maybe 32 or 33.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ingrid, oddly. She's brilliant, but she's 50 and she doesn't want anything to do with the AI stuff, she says it's cheating. People like her know the machines better than anyone and they might be the slowest to move.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to make a plan and urge co-workers to learn the robots while they're still needed to run them. He'd say it calmly.
S3.think: He expects three or four good years in robot cells and set-ups, more if he starts his own business. After that he's unsure, but he'd have savings for once.
S3.do: Joins the robot cell in year one and takes a weekend robot programming course. Starts a side business installing and fixing small robot arms for local workshops in year two and saves at least two hundred a month, keeping the e-bike sales for cash.
S3.feel: Mostly busy and excited, with unease in the background.
S3.quote: She's brilliant, but she's 50 and she doesn't want anything to do with the AI stuff, she says it's cheating.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him build a small business and a real cushion for the first time. He'd push back plans for children to save first. He worries for skilled older workers who refuse the tools, not for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to. That sounds harsh, so I'd probably soften it. But I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly good news. Ten years is long enough to get skilled, build a little business and put money aside. I'd be 37 when it lands, and I'd want to be someone who owns a bit of it, not just someone it happens to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the robot cell over the next year, then the programming course. Within three or four years I'd want my own small set-up business, maybe with one van and one helper. Any spare money I'd put into it, tools, a small workshop, maybe shares in the robot companies if I ever have enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't use the ten years is choosing not to. Is that fair to someone like Ingrid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. You're right. Some people can't just switch, they've got kids, or bad backs, or they're 55. I'd still say it's worth trying, but I wouldn't say it to her face like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your business once AGI does arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably it gets squeezed too, eventually. I'm not stupid. But if I own the tools and the van and a few clients, I've got something to sell or something to fall back on, which is more than I've got now.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty and anyone who doesn't use it is choosing not to, though he'd soften that in practice.
S4.think: He sees it as mostly good news: time to gain skills, build a small business and save. At 37 he wants to own part of it, not just have it happen to him.
S4.do: Learns the robot cell over the next year, then takes the programming course, aiming for his own small set-up business with a van and a helper within three or four years. Puts spare money into tools, a workshop and possibly shares in robot companies.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, even a bit hopeful.
S4.quote: I'd want to be someone who owns a bit of it, not just someone it happens to.
S4.fieldNote: A decade makes him optimistic and ambitious about ownership. When challenged, he quickly concedes his harsh remark was unfair to people with fewer choices. He knows his business would be squeezed eventually but values having assets.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. Everything else gives me time to get ahead, that one doesn't. What would help is the government keeping rent and food covered for a year or two, so people like me can try something new without going under.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the side stuff. Loads of people on the shop floor have a little hustle, fixing cars, doing nails, selling stuff. That's where people are actually trying things out with AI, not at work, because at work nobody asks us.

headlineQuote: That's where people are actually trying things out with AI, not at work, because at work nobody asks us.
portrait: Karl Fischer is a 27-year-old press brake operator in an appliance factory's sheet metal shop, five months in and still slow at setups. He uses AI every day, both to learn the bending tables and to run a small side business refurbishing e-bikes. Steady change and even the ten-year AGI picture look like openings to him, with a plan to move onto the robot cell and later run his own robot set-up business. Fast AGI makes him nervous but he still hunts for a short window rather than freezing. He blames no one and leans towards government help only when everyone is hit at once.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's the only picture that doesn't give him time to get ahead.
whatWouldHelp: Government covering rent and food for a year or two so people can try something new without going under.
